## Short answer

and blue parasols, the parked white van, the pink "meat & dairy pavilion" and the
crowd further up the market. He would have to stop and look back over his shoulder
to see the bread at all.

## Who is who in the picture

* **The man with the bicycle (left of frame).** He is the older, heavier man with
  short grey hair, in a light grey/white short-sleeved polo shirt and loose dark
  navy trousers and sandals, pushing a **red bicycle** along on his right-hand side
  with a dark jacket or bag draped over his other forearm.
* **The striped umbrella and the bread.** Across the top centre-left of the frame is
  a row of big **purple/magenta-and-white striped market umbrellas**. Its pole comes
  down immediately beside the young man in the white **"PRADA" T-shirt** in the right
  foreground, who is handing over / stacking a pile of round Central Asian flatbread
  (*non* / *lepyoshka*). A lad in a white vest stands with him behind trestle tables
  and handcarts heaped with the same loaves. This is the bread stand in question, and
  it sits only a metre or two from the photographer.

## Which way is he currently travelling?

He is unambiguously walking **towards the camera / the viewer**:

* We see his face and the front of his shirt; he is looking straight down the lens.
* We see the **front** of the bicycle — the front wheel is the part nearest us at the
  bottom of the frame, with the handlebars turned towards us and his hand on the grip.
* He is caught mid-stride, one sandalled foot swung forward, with the toes of both
  feet pointing at the camera.

So he is coming *out* of the aisle behind him and *towards* the open, paved area where
the photographer — and the striped-umbrella bread stand — are standing.

## The spatial reasoning

Working from the apparent sizes and the position of the horizon, the cyclist is roughly
4 m from the camera, while the bread seller under the striped umbrella is only about
1.5 m from it and about 30–35° round the panorama from the cyclist. Putting those on a
plan view, the bread stand lies only about **15–20° off the cyclist's current line of
travel** — essentially straight ahead of him, slightly to his left. That matches what
the photograph shows: from where he stands the row of bread carts is already visible in
front of him, only partly screened by the woman in the black dress carrying the red bag

Reverse that heading and the same stand ends up about **160–165° away from where he is
facing** — i.e. directly behind him. A person cannot see behind their own back, so the
answer is no.

## One honest qualification

The bread market is not a single point but a **long row** of vendors and handcarts
running under that line of striped umbrellas, stretching from right beside the camera
back into the middle distance (you can see two or three further carts of loaves about

umbrella** — the man in the PRADA T-shirt with the stack of bread and the tables of
loaves next to him — because that is on the camera side of him, behind him once he
reverses.

**Conclusion: travelling in the opposite direction would take him away from that bread
stand, not towards it, and he would not have a clear view of it.**
